Apollo 13. On April 11, 1970, NASA launched Apollo 13 with the goal of landing on the Moon near the Fra Mauro crater. The crew—James Lovell, Jack Swigert, and Fred Haise—were prepared for a routine lunar mission. Two days into the flight, everything changed.

On April 13, an oxygen tank rupture in the service module forced mission control to abort the lunar landing and work toward returning the crew safely to Earth. Astronaut Jack Swigert transmitted the now-famous understatement: "Houston, we've had a problem."

The three astronauts sheltered in the lunar module, using it as a lifeboat to return home instead of as a landing vehicle. Mission control and the crew made a series of improvised fixes, including adapting parts from the command module to improvise a carbon-dioxide filter. The resourcefulness demonstrated during this crisis was extraordinary. The astronauts endured extreme cold and power rationing, managing critical life-support challenges that would have defeated lesser teams.

On April 17, the three astronauts splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean. The mission demonstrated the effectiveness of astronaut training, ground support, and collaborative problem-solving under extreme pressure. James Lovell navigated the return, drawing on his experience and composure. Mission control, the ground team that solved the crisis moment by moment, proved itself indispensable to human spaceflight. Apollo 13 became not a failure but a triumph of human ingenuity.
